Making code able to support many locales

options: The layout is mirrored (e.g. navigation and icons with direction)
Mixed content such as numbers and English product names displays correctly
`dir="rtl"` is set on the page or relevant elements
Phone numbers are reversed digit by digit

questions.prompt: Dates show as 03/04/2026 to all users. A UK user reads it as 3 April, a US user as 4 March. What should you recommend?
options: Format dates per user locale (or an unambiguous format such as 3 Apr 2026 / ISO 8601 where appropriate)
questions.explanation: Locale-aware formatting (Intl.DateTimeFormat) or unambiguous formats prevent misreading.

questions.prompt: A message is built as `count + ' file' + (count === 1 ? '' : 's') + ' deleted'`. Translators for Polish and Arabic complain. Why?
options: Plural rules differ by language (Polish has several forms; Arabic has six categories); use ICU MessageFormat / Intl.PluralRules with per-locale forms
Only the word order is wrong
questions.explanation: English's one/other rule does not generalise. CLDR plural categories (zero, one, two, few, many, other) handled by the i18n library solve this.

questions.prompt: Search for "cafe" does not find "Café" entered by a French user, and sorting puts "Zoë" before "Ångström" in a Swedish list where Å should come after Z. What do these show?
options: Missing Unicode normalisation/accent-insensitive search and locale-unaware collation; use proper normalisation and locale-aware sorting (e.g. Intl.Collator)
questions.explanation: Text comparison needs normalisation (NFC/NFD, accent folding where wanted) and sorting needs the locale's collation rules.

coding.title: Pseudo-localize a string
coding.prompt:
Write `pseudo(text)` that returns `'[' + transformed + ' ' + '~'.repeat(n) + ']'`, where `transformed` replaces a→à, e→é, i→î, o→ö, u→ü (lower case only), and `n` is `Math.ceil(text.length * 0.3)`. Text inside `{curly}` placeholders must be left unchanged.

Example: `pseudo('Save {count} files')` returns `'[Sàvé {count} fîlés ~~~~~~]'`.
coding.explanation: Accents prove the string went through the translation pipeline and the font supports them; padding simulates expansion; brackets show truncation. Placeholders must stay intact or the app breaks at runtime.
hints: Walk the characters and track whether you are inside braces.
Padding length uses the original text length.

coding.title: Choose plural forms with Intl.PluralRules
coding.prompt:
Write `message(locale, count, forms)` where `forms` maps CLDR plural categories (`one`, `few`, `many`, `other`, ...) to templates containing `#`. Use `new Intl.PluralRules(locale).select(count)` to pick the category (falling back to `other`) and replace `#` with the count.

Example: `message('pl', 5, {one: '# plik', few: '# pliki', many: '# plików', other: '# pliku'})` returns `'5 plików'`.
coding.explanation: Intl.PluralRules knows each locale's CLDR rules: Polish uses 'few' for 2-4 (but not 12-14) and 'many' for 5+. Tests across 1, 2, 5, 12, 22 catch hand-written rules that only handle one/other.

tests.name: Polish forms
tests.code:
const f = {one: '# plik', few: '# pliki', many: '# plików', other: '# pliku'};
assertEqual([1, 2, 5, 12, 22].map((n) => message('pl', n, f)), ['1 plik', '2 pliki', '5 plików', '12 plików', '22 pliki']);

tests.name: English
tests.code:
assertEqual(message('en', 1, {one: '# file', other: '# files'}), '1 file');
assertEqual(message('en', 0, {one: '# file', other: '# files'}), '0 files');
